messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor\). We need

\[
n\mid (k!)^{n!}+450.
\]

Let \(p^a\|n\).

### 1. Prime factors \(p\le k\)

Then \(p\mid k!\), so \(p^{n!}\mid (k!)^{n!}\). Since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(a\le n!\), hence \(p^a\mid (k!)^{n!}\). Therefore

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

Thus any such prime factor of \(n\) must be \(2,3,5\), with exponents at most those in

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

### 2. Prime factors \(p>k\)

Then \(p\nmid k!\). Also \(p\mid n\), so \(p\le n\), which implies \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat,

\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

So any prime factor larger than \(k\) must be \(11\) or \(41\), and only to the first power.

Hence every valid \(n\) divides

\[
2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\cdot 11\cdot 41.
\]

If \(11\mid n\), then \(11>k\), so \(n\le 120\).  
If \(41\mid n\), then \(41>k\), so \(n\le 1680\).  
They cannot both divide \(n\).

If \(41\mid n\), write \(n=41d\) with \(d\mid 450\). Since \(41d\le 1680\), \(d\le 40\). The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\), giving \(n\le 41\cdot 30=1230\).

Now check \(n=1230\). Here \(\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35\), and

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

- Modulo \(2,3,5\): \(35!\equiv 0\) and \(450\equiv 0\), so the sum is \(0\).
- Modulo \(41\): \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), so by Fermat,

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Also \(450\equiv -1\pmod{41}\), so the sum is \(0\pmod{41}\).

Thus \(1230\) works, and no larger integer can work.

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
